historical_record.description: St. John's Presbyterian Church, a shingle church designed by the firm Dodge & Dolliver. San Francisco Landmark No. 83.

Arthur V. Foster, a broker and philanthropist who had joined the congregation in 1875, assembled the corner lot at Arguello and Lake — two lots on Arguello and a fifty-foot slice of an unsubdivided 125-foot Lake Street frontage — in time for the architects to draw up a church. The plot is the shape it still is: 135 feet on Lake, 74 feet 7½ inches on Arguello, doglegging round a neighbouring parcel to the south.
Ground was broken for the church.

The church was built to a design by Dodge & Dolliver — a partnership of about four years, and this its one substantial work — in the Shingle Style outside and Gothic within, because the donor who paid for land and building required the interior of the congregation's two earlier churches to be re-created. Much of it was: the arch spanning the pulpit with its inscription, the pews, the pulpit furnishings, the narthex rose window, interior woodwork and eight stained glass windows were all carried over. The two largest, in the cross-gabled walls, are dedicated to the congregation's founding trustee Henry Mayo Newhall and to its first pastor, William Anderson Scott.

Four days after the new church was dedicated, the earthquake brought a chimney down on the organ at the west end of the building, breaking trackers, squares and roller boards and crushing pipes; it took several weeks to put right.
A one-storey Sunday school was added in the yard behind the neighbouring Arguello Boulevard parcel, on the strip of lot that runs 27½ feet further south.
A second storey was put on the southerly addition, holding a chapel that took one of the older stained glass windows.
A permit records fire damage in the auditorium beneath the chapel, with millwork, plaster and flooring to be replaced; a 1961 permit replaced the auditorium's wood floor with concrete.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places as the oldest church left in the Richmond District and its only one in the Shingle Style — the last standing sign that San Francisco's congregations followed the city west at the turn of the century.

A three-manual Johnson organ of thirty stops, bought for $10,000 and shipped round Cape Horn from Westfield, Massachusetts, was installed in the congregation's first church; it moved with them in 1889 and again to this building. Thirty of the forty ranks of pipes now in it were first heard that year. It has been overhauled several times since and keeps its massive black walnut case.
